Investing in scheduling and instrumentation is reversible in the best sense: the skills, tooling, and monitoring we build retain their value regardless of what we later decide, and if the work reveals that our demand genuinely exceeds capacity, we will then buy with much better evidence about what to buy and how much. The utilisation path is not merely cheaper; it is an information-generating investment that de-risks the purchase we may eventually need to make.

So my recommendation is this: defer the purchase for one quarter, commit two engineers to the scheduling and instrumentation work, and set a concrete trigger — sustained utilisation above 75% with queue-time SLA breaches — at which we buy without further debate. I hold this recommendation with real uncertainty. If the product team's latency commitments are harder than I believe, or if the scheduler work stalls, we should revisit within six weeks rather than waiting out the quarter. Utilization improvements, by contrast, are mostly reversible and compounding — better batching, smarter scheduling, and quantization of the two models that dominate our memory footprint are changes we can tune, undo, or extend, and the tooling we build keeps paying off regardless of how our fleet grows. Buying hardware now, before we understand our own load, risks provisioning for a moment rather than a trend.

Let's be fair to the "just buy more" position. But that framing hides most of the cost. The purchase price is the smallest part of owning hardware. There's power and cooling, rack space, the operational burden of a larger and more heterogeneous fleet, and — most importantly — the depreciation question. GPUs lose value quickly, and buying now locks us into today's guess about our workload shape. If our traffic mix changes, or if we shift more inference to a hosted provider as our contracts allow, that hardware becomes stranded capacity we're paying to house and power.

There's also the opportunity cost to weigh honestly. The engineering effort to buy, install, and integrate new cards is not trivial, and every hour spent on procurement is an hour not spent on the product work that actually differentiates us. Meanwhile, our utilisation data tells a story: our fleet averages well under 40% utilisation across the day, with sharp peaks and long troughs. The problem isn't that we lack capacity — it's that our capacity is badly shaped. Batch sizes are conservative, models are loaded redundantly across nodes, and we have no mechanism for preemption or priority scheduling, so a batch job can block an interactive request.

## What better utilisation looks like

Concretely, I'd propose we spend the next quarter on three fronts, treated as one coherent effort rather than a list of side projects. First, dynamic batching and request coalescing, which our own profiling suggests could absorb most of our peak-hour queueing. Second, a proper scheduler with priorities, so interactive traffic always preempts background work — this directly addresses the latency problem without adding a single card. Third, consolidating model replicas and sharing weights across processes to free memory we're currently wasting. None of this is exotic; it's standard practice at every team that runs inference at scale, and we've simply deferred it because hardware was easy to buy.

Two more considerations tilt me this way. On reliability: a larger fleet is a larger failure surface. Against: every layer we add between requests and silicon is a new failure mode, and our current direct-to-GPU setup, however crude, is simple and predictable. Our current fleet runs at roughly 35–40% average utilisation, with peaks that occasionally saturate individual nodes. That gap between average and peak is the crux of the whole question. If our machines were genuinely pegged most of the day, buying more would be an easy call. They aren't. The saturation we experience is concentrated in predictable windows — batch inference jobs, scheduled fine-tuning runs, and the mid-afternoon evaluation queue — and much of the rest of the time expensive hardware sits idle. Idle capital is the quietest form of waste in our budget, and right now we're carrying a lot of it.

**The cost picture**

A meaningful hardware expansion would cost somewhere in the low six figures once you include the cards themselves, power delivery, cooling, and the rack space we'd need to find. That's not an impossible sum, but it's a sum that competes directly with other things we've said we want: headcount, a proper observability stack, and the latency work on the customer-facing inference path. Opportunity cost is real here. Every dollar spent on GPUs we don't yet need is a dollar not spent on something that might compound faster. And hardware depreciates. GPU generations turn over quickly, and a purchase made today to solve a peak-load problem we might solve with scheduling will be worth a fraction of its price in eighteen months.

**Latency and reliability**

The strongest argument for more hardware is latency. Interactive workloads do suffer when batch jobs crowd the queue, and p95 latency has degraded in the last two months. But we should be honest about the cause: it's contention, not capacity. A scheduler that separates interactive from batch traffic, plus a modest reservation policy, would likely recover most of the latency we've lost without adding a single card. There's a reliability angle too, and it cuts both ways. More hardware means more redundancy — a node failure hurts less when you have slack. But our current fleet is homogeneous enough that a single failure today already degrades us gracefully; the marginal reliability gain from additional nodes is smaller than it first appears, and every added node is also an added failure surface to maintain.

**Reversibility**

This is the consideration that most shapes our recommendation. Improving utilisation is a reversible, low-regret investment. If we build better scheduling, queueing, and batching and it turns out we were wrong — that we truly are capacity-constrained — we've lost a few weeks of engineering time and we've gained infrastructure we'd want anyway. Buying hardware is the opposite: it's a largely irreversible commitment of capital and physical space, and unwinding it is slow and lossy. When two options are plausibly similar in benefit, the reversible one should win, especially at our stage of uncertainty about where workloads are heading. Model sizes, inference patterns, and even our own product direction could shift enough in six months to change what "enough capacity" means.

**What we're uncertain about**

We want to be candid about the limits of this analysis. Our utilisation numbers come from coarse instrumentation, and it's possible that "35–40%" masks hot spots where individual teams are genuinely starved. If that's true, the fairness problem is real even if the capacity problem isn't, and we should solve it with better allocation rather than more metal. We also can't fully predict demand growth; if a new initiative lands hard in Q3, our calculus changes. That's precisely why we're proposing a decision checkpoint rather than a permanent deferral.

**Recommendation**

Spend the next eight to ten weeks on utilisation: a proper scheduler separating interactive and batch traffic, instrumentation good enough to trust, and queueing policies that protect latency-sensitive work. Set a review at the end of that period with explicit thresholds — sustained utilisation above 70%, or p95 latency still failing targets under a fair scheduler — that would trigger a purchase proposal with our full confidence behind it. If the numbers say we need hardware then, we'll buy it and be glad we waited. If they don't, we'll have saved a significant sum and learned something about our own systems in the process.

The cheap, reversible experiment first. The expensive, permanent one only if the evidence demands it.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** Recommendation on our local AI hardware capacity question

We've been asked to decide whether to purchase additional GPU hardware for our local inference and training workloads, or to invest in improving utilisation of the machines we already own. After several weeks of measurement, back-of-envelope costing, and honest argument among ourselves, we're recommending the second option: spend the next quarter improving utilisation of our existing fleet, and defer the purchase decision until we have evidence we actually need it. Here's the reasoning, including where we could still be wrong.

First, the cost picture. Our current fleet sits at roughly 35–40% average utilisation, with sharp peaks around model evaluation runs and long troughs overnight and on weekends. The capital cost of adding capacity is not just the hardware itself — it's the rack space, power provisioning, cooling headroom, and the ongoing operational burden of more machines to patch and monitor. Against that, the cost of better utilisation is mostly engineering time: a proper scheduler, queueing discipline for batch jobs, and some work on model quantisation and batching so that inference requests pack more densely onto the silicon we have. Our rough estimate is that pushing average utilisation to 65–70% would defer the need for new hardware by at least two quarters, possibly longer, at perhaps a tenth of the cost of the purchase. That asymmetry is hard to argue with.

Latency is the strongest argument on the other side, and we want to treat it seriously rather than wave it away. Right now, interactive workloads occasionally queue behind batch jobs, and p95 latency suffers as a result. Buying more hardware would make that problem disappear by brute force. But it's the wrong first response, because the latency problem is largely self-inflicted: batch jobs and interactive requests share the same GPUs with no isolation. Workload partitioning — dedicating specific cards or time slices to latency-sensitive traffic — would fix most of it without new capacity. If, after partitioning, we still see p95 latency above our target during peak hours, that becomes a genuine signal of a capacity shortfall, and we should revisit the purchase with real data in hand.

Reliability cuts both ways, and we should be honest about that too. A larger fleet gives us more redundancy; a single failed node is a smaller fraction of total capacity. Our current fleet is small enough that one dead GPU is a noticeable event. However, better utilisation done well usually improves reliability rather than degrading it, because it forces us to build proper scheduling, health checks, and failover behaviour — infrastructure we'd need regardless of fleet size. The purchase path, by contrast, tends to add machines without adding resilience discipline, which just means more things that can break in more ways.

The opportunity cost question is the one that most changed our minds. The engineering time that a hardware purchase would consume — procurement, integration, capacity planning for power and cooling — is time not spent on the product work that actually differentiates us. Meanwhile, the utilisation work (scheduling, batching, quantisation) produces skills and infrastructure that compound: they make any future hardware we do buy more effective, and they make us better at capacity planning generally. Money spent on underused GPUs is money spent on idle silicon; money spent on utilisation is money spent on capability.

Finally, reversibility. Buying hardware is close to irreversible in practice. GPUs depreciate quickly, resale is messy, and the power and rack commitments are sticky. Improving utilisation is almost entirely reversible — if a scheduling change hurts latency, we roll it back; if quantisation degrades output quality beyond an acceptable threshold, we revert to full precision. When two options are roughly comparable on immediate benefit, the reversible one is almost always the right place to start, because it preserves our ability to change course as we learn.

Where could we be wrong? If our workload grows faster than forecast — say, a new customer commitment or a large training run lands next quarter — utilisation improvements won't keep up, and we'd be buying hardware under time pressure, which is when bad purchases happen. We therefore propose a tripwire: if sustained utilisation exceeds 75% for two consecutive weeks, or if we can't meet latency targets after partitioning, we escalate the purchase request immediately rather than waiting out the quarter.

In short: measure before we buy, fix the scheduling and batching problems we already own, and keep the purchase option open with clear triggers for when to exercise it. We'll report back with utilisation and latency data at the end of the quarter.

Nobody has a strong incentive to release a reservation because there's no cost to holding one. These are the classic symptoms of a cluster that has grown organically without anyone owning the scheduling layer, and they are fixable.

Fixing them is cheap in money and expensive in attention. Better queueing, a shared reservation policy with automatic expiry, and a nightly batch window would probably take one engineer six to eight weeks of focused work, some of it unglamorous. The payoff is uncertain but plausibly large: if we can lift sustained utilisation from the low thirties to the fifties, we have effectively doubled our fleet without spending anything on hardware. Hardware is the most visible need but not obviously the highest-value one, and capital spent on silicon is largely irrecoverable — a GPU we buy this year will be worth a fraction of its price in two years and will be slow relative to whatever ships next. Improving utilisation, by contrast, is a reversible investment. If we build the scheduling layer and it turns out we still need more capacity, nothing is wasted; the tooling makes the new hardware more valuable too. If we buy hardware and the shortage turns out to be a scheduling artifact, we've spent real money to preserve a bad habit.

The instinctive response is to buy more cards. That instinct deserves scrutiny, because in our experience "the cluster feels slow" and "the cluster is fully utilised" are frequently different claims.

Our monitoring gives us coarse-grained GPU utilisation percentages, but those numbers are notoriously misleading. A card can report 80% "utilisation" while doing memory-bound work at a fraction of its theoretical throughput. We do not currently have a reliable picture of how much useful computation we are extracting per dollar of hardware we already own. Before we spend on new capacity, we should know whether the constraint is genuinely compute, or whether it is memory bandwidth, model placement, scheduling overhead, or simply poor job packing — for instance, small inference models co-resident with large training jobs that fragment memory and force idle time.

There are several concrete interventions we believe will help. Better batching of inference requests typically yields large gains at modest latency cost, and we have never systematically tuned our batch sizes against our actual traffic distribution. Smarter scheduling — separating batch and interactive workloads, or time-slicing them with clear priority — could relieve the contention that engineers experience as "waiting for the cluster." Quantisation or more aggressive model compression for serving could free memory and throughput on cards that are currently over-provisioned for the models they run. None of this is glamorous, but each item is cheap, and the total cost is a fraction of even one additional high-end accelerator.

**The cost of buying now**

A meaningful hardware purchase is expensive not only in capital but in opportunity cost. The money spent on accelerators is money not spent on engineering headcount, evaluation tooling, or the observability work that would benefit us regardless of what we own. Hardware also carries hidden carrying costs: power, cooling, rack space, and the operational burden of integrating new cards into our stack. And the market moves quickly — hardware bought today at premium prices may be worth materially less in eighteen months, both in resale value and relative capability. Buying is also a commitment that is difficult to reverse; utilisation improvements, by contrast, cost mostly engineering time and can be abandoned if they stop paying off.

**Reliability and latency considerations**

We should be honest that utilisation gains have limits. If we push the fleet harder, we reduce headroom, and headroom is what absorbs traffic spikes and hardware failures. A cluster running at 95% effective utilisation is fragile: one failed card means degraded service rather than mild slowness. Any utilisation push must therefore be paired with explicit reliability targets — a defined latency SLO for interactive traffic and a reserve capacity policy for batch work. If we cannot meet those targets with the existing fleet even after optimisation, that is precisely the evidence that justifies a purchase.

**Uncertainty**

We acknowledge real uncertainty here. Our demand forecast is weak; if a new product initiative lands in the next quarter, our inference load could double, and the utilisation argument would collapse quickly. Conversely, if our traffic is flat, buying hardware now would strand capital. The six-to-eight-week utilisation effort doubles as a demand-observation window, which reduces this uncertainty at low cost.

**Next steps**

We propose a small task group to instrument the fleet properly, run batching and scheduling experiments, and report back with measured numbers and a revised capacity recommendation. If the data says we need hardware, we will ask for it with confidence — and with a much better sense of how much.

I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the answer is less obvious than the purchase order makes it look.

The case for buying is straightforward and I don't want to dismiss it. Our p99 latency on the shared inference box has crept up over the last two months, mostly because batch queues form whenever two or three heavy jobs land at once. That latency is not free — it shows up as slower iteration for the people doing model evaluation, and slow iteration is the kind of tax that compounds quietly. Every hour someone waits for a queue to drain is an hour they spend context-switching instead of experimenting. If our real bottleneck is creative throughput rather than compute throughput, more hardware buys back attention, and attention is the scarcest thing we have.

But before we conclude that the queue is a capacity problem, we should be honest about how much of it is a utilisation problem. Right now our fleet idles a substantial fraction of the day. Jobs are scheduled manually, nobody has built a proper queue with priorities, and several long-running fine-tunes hog memory they no longer need because nobody wrote the cleanup job. The utilisation work — a scheduler, memory accounting, maybe quantised serving for the smaller models — is maybe three to four weeks of one engineer's time. The hardware option is roughly the same cost in cash, but nearly zero engineering time. So the real trade is money versus focus, and that's the framing I'd like us to deliberate on rather than "buy or not buy."

Here's the asymmetry that tips me. The utilisation work is reversible and general. If we build a scheduler and it turns out we still need more hardware, we've lost a few weeks and gained infrastructure that makes the new hardware more valuable too — a bigger fleet without scheduling discipline just means a bigger queue. The purchase, by contrast, is largely irreversible in practice. Accelerators depreciate fast, resale is a hassle, and once the budget is spent it's spent. Reversibility matters most when we're uncertain, and we are genuinely uncertain: our workload mix may shift toward API-based models for the routine stuff, in which case local capacity matters less in six months than it does today. Spending down our flexibility now to solve a problem that better software might solve for free is the wrong side of that bet.

There's also an opportunity cost that's easy to miss. The engineer who would own the utilisation work is the same person who best understands our serving stack. Concretely, I'd propose we spend two to three engineer-weeks on three things: a proper job queue with priority classes so batch workloads yield to interactive ones; model warm-pooling so we stop paying 40–90 second cold-start penalties on every request; and consolidating our smaller experiments onto a shared scheduler instead of people grabbing whichever card is free. If the model mix shifts, or if hosted inference pricing continues to fall, hardware bought now to solve today's problem may be poorly matched to next year's.

That last point leads to reversibility, and it's where I land most firmly. Buying hardware is close to irreversible at our scale: resale value is poor, and the machine will sit in our rack whether or not it's the right answer. Improving utilisation is highly reversible — we can stop, adjust, or abandon the approach at any point without stranded capital. When two options are roughly comparable on immediate benefit, the reversible one is almost always worth taking first, because it buys information cheaply. If we spend a quarter on utilisation and still see genuine saturation, we'll make the purchase case with real data instead of anxiety, and we'll know exactly what class of capacity we need.

So my recommendation: commit the next quarter to the utilisation work, with a target of fifty-five percent sustained utilisation and no regression on interactive p99 latency, and hold the hardware purchase as a pre-approved fallback if we miss that target or if demand growth outruns us. I want to be clear about the uncertainty here — my utilisation figures come from a single week of telemetry and could be flattering, and I may be underestimating how much engineering time the scheduling work will absorb. If anyone has evidence that contention is already hurting user-facing reliability in ways our dashboards don't show, that would change my calculus, and I'd rather hear it Thursday than after we've committed.

The hardware will still be for sale in three months. Let's make sure we're buying it for the right reasons when we do.

## Summary

We've been asked whether we should purchase additional local GPU hardware or invest in improving utilisation of the four A100-class nodes we already own. After several weeks of measurement and discussion, our recommendation is to improve utilisation first, and defer any purchase decision by at least one quarter. The case for buying is real, but it is weaker than it first appears, and the option to buy later does not expire.

## What the data shows

Our utilisation telemetry tells a more encouraging story than our intuition did. Across the last eight weeks, average GPU occupancy sits at roughly 38%, but that number hides a bimodal pattern. During weekday business hours, when the fine-tuning queue and the interactive notebooks compete for the same nodes, utilisation spikes above 85% and we see queue waits of up to three hours. Overnight and on weekends, the fleet idles near 12%. In other words, we do not have a capacity problem so much as a scheduling problem: the hardware we need exists, but it is in the wrong place at the wrong time.

The cheapest interventions are also the most obvious. A simple reservation system for interactive work, a batch queue that drains overnight, and automatic checkpointing so long jobs can be preempted would, by our estimate, push effective utilisation above 60% without buying anything. That is roughly the threshold at which our current queue-wait complaints disappear. The engineering cost is modest — perhaps three weeks of one engineer's time — and the work is useful regardless of what we decide later, since any future fleet, purchased or rented, will need the same tooling.

## The case for buying, and why we're not persuaded yet

The argument for new hardware is not frivolous. Our latency-sensitive workloads — the internal copilot deployment and the retrieval service — currently share nodes with batch jobs, and contention produces p99 latency spikes that have caused two on-call incidents this quarter. Dedicated hardware for serving would fix that. It would also give us headroom for the evaluation work planned next quarter, which we cannot currently schedule without displacing training runs.

But the purchase case rests on assumptions we should stress-test. First, cost: a new node is not just its sticker price. Power, cooling, rack space, and — most importantly — the ongoing operational burden of a heterogeneous fleet all add up, and our finance colleagues estimate total cost of ownership roughly 1.6 times the capital figure over three years. Second, opportunity cost: the same budget would fund roughly two quarters of a contractor who could deliver the scheduling work plus several other backlog items, or a reserved cloud allocation that would cover our peak needs while we learn more. Third, and most importantly, reversibility: hardware is the least reversible option on the table. Once bought, it depreciates whether we use it or not, and if our workload mix shifts — which it is likely to, given the roadmap — we may find ourselves owning capacity optimised for a problem we no longer have. Cloud capacity, by contrast, can be resized or dropped. Scheduling software is reversible in the sense that it costs only the time to build it.

There is also a reliability argument that cuts both ways. More nodes means more failure domains, and our current maintenance process is already stretched thin. Better utilisation of a smaller fleet means each node gets more attention, and our mean time to repair — currently poor — is more likely to improve.

## What we recommend

Concretely: fund the scheduling and queueing work now, treat it as a three-week experiment with clear success criteria (p99 serving latency under contention, queue wait times, sustained utilisation), and revisit the purchase question at the end of the quarter with better data. If utilisation improvements stall below 55%, or if serving latency remains unacceptable, we will have lost little and learned a great deal, and the purchase case will be stronger and better evidenced.

## Uncertainty

We want to be honest about what we don't know. Our utilisation projections assume demand stays roughly flat, and the roadmap suggests it may not. If the evaluation programme grows faster than planned, the calculus changes, and we should not let sunk effort in scheduling work bias us against hardware when the time comes. We also have limited visibility into cloud pricing trends, which affect the buy-versus-rent comparison. The recommendation above is the best decision given current information, not a permanent position — and the whole point of sequencing it this way is that we will be better placed to revise it.

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure team
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been asked to settle a question that has come up repeatedly in the last month: do we purchase additional local AI hardware, or do we invest in raising the utilisation of the machines we already own? I want to lay out our thinking and make a recommendation, with the caveat that some of what follows rests on assumptions we should treat as provisional.

The immediate trigger is familiar. Our batch inference queues have been backing up during peak hours, and two recent product demos were affected by latency spikes that embarrassed us in front of stakeholders. The instinctive response — "just buy more GPUs" — is understandable, and it would work. But instinct is not a plan, and the numbers suggest instinct would be expensive here.

Start with utilisation. When we instrumented the fleet properly last week, we found our headline utilisation figure of 60 percent was misleading. That number counts any period in which a job is resident on a card, but much of that time is spent on model loading, checkpoint writes, and idle waiting between micro-batches. Effective utilisation — time spent actually producing tokens or embeddings — is closer to 35 percent. The gap is not mysterious. Our scheduler still assigns work statically, models are loaded and evicted far more often than necessary because of memory fragmentation, and several long-running jobs were sized for hardware we no longer own. None of this is a hardware problem. It is an orchestration problem, and orchestration problems are cheap to fix relative to the alternative.

The cost comparison makes this concrete. The hardware option on the table — two additional high-memory accelerators plus the networking and power work to accommodate them — comes to roughly $180,000 in capital, plus a meaningful increase in our monthly power and colocation bill, plus the engineering time to integrate and monitor the new capacity. The utilisation option is primarily staff time: perhaps six weeks of focused work from two engineers to implement dynamic batching, improve model caching, and fix the scheduler's placement logic. Even at fully loaded cost, that is an order of magnitude cheaper. If we recover even half of the wasted capacity, we defer the hardware purchase by at least two quarters, possibly longer.

Latency deserves its own consideration, because it is the one place where the two options are not equivalent. Better scheduling and batching will reduce queue-induced latency, which is the dominant component of our tail latency today. But if demand grows faster than we expect, software optimisation alone cannot create capacity that does not exist. There is a floor below which clever orchestration cannot dig us out. Our forecast says demand grows roughly 40 percent over the next two quarters; recovering 25 points of utilisation on existing hardware covers that growth with margin, but the forecast has real uncertainty attached, and I want to be honest about that rather than pretend the model is precise.

Reliability cuts in favour of the utilisation path in one respect and against it in another. Buying more hardware increases redundancy — a card failure today degrades us noticeably, and a second pool would cushion that. On the other hand, the reliability problems we actually experience are mostly software-induced: jobs wedged in bad states, memory leaks forcing restarts, scheduler deadlocks. More hardware does not fix those; it multiplies the surface on which they occur. Fixing the orchestration layer improves reliability and capacity simultaneously, which is the strongest argument for doing it first.

There is also opportunity cost and reversibility to weigh. Capital spent on accelerators is largely sunk; resale markets for used AI hardware are volatile, and the pace of hardware improvement means today's purchase may look poor value within a year. Engineering time spent on our scheduling stack is not wasted even if we later buy hardware — the improvements carry forward and make any future fleet cheaper to run. In other words, the utilisation investment is robust to being wrong; the hardware purchase is only optimal if our demand forecast is right and our current inefficiency is irreducible. We have good evidence it is not irreducible.

So the recommendation is: fund the utilisation work now, with a defined scope and a hard checkpoint. If, after the orchestration improvements land, our effective utilisation exceeds 55 percent and queue latency still breaches our SLO under forecast load, we bring the hardware proposal back with better data and my support. That checkpoint keeps the hardware option open without paying for it prematurely, and it converts a debate about instincts into a decision we can make on evidence.

I'm happy to walk through the instrumentation data with anyone who wants the detail.

Buying more cards before we fix scheduling would mean paying full price to solve the easy half of the problem while leaving the hard half intact.

The cost picture reinforces this. Capital purchase is only the visible line item. New cards bring power, cooling, rack space, and — less glamorously — a maintenance and driver-burden cost that our small team feels acutely. Every additional machine is something we must patch, monitor, and eventually decommission. Improving utilisation, by contrast, is mostly engineering time we would spend anyway: better job queueing, batching small inference requests, time-slicing between training and serving workloads, and tightening the handoff between teams so a job doesn't hold a card while its author is at lunch. The opportunity cost asymmetry is stark. Money spent on hardware is money not spent on headcount, tooling, or the reliability work we keep deferring; time spent on utilisation produces skills and infrastructure that compound regardless of what we later buy.

Latency deserves honest treatment, because it is the one place where the buy-more argument has real force. If our serving latency degrades because inference requests contend for scarce accelerators, no amount of clever scheduling fully rescues the tail. Batching improves throughput but can add milliseconds that users notice. So the right move is to measure first: if p99 latency for our primary service is already within tolerance and the pain is confined to internal batch work, utilisation work is clearly sufficient. If we find that user-facing latency is genuinely suffering at current load, that changes the calculus, and I'd be the first to say so. My suspicion, based on the complaint pattern — mostly about queue waits, rarely about user-facing latency — is that the pain is internal, and internal pain is cheap to relieve.

Reliability cuts the other way, and it's the strongest argument I've heard for buying. Our fleet is small enough that a single machine failure removes a meaningful fraction of capacity, and redundancy is a legitimate reason to hold more hardware than average demand requires. But redundancy can be bought gradually, and it can also be partly achieved through better failover: checkpointing jobs so they resume on another card, and pre-emptible scheduling so a hardware fault degrades service rather than halting it. Finally, reversibility. Buying hardware is nearly irreversible at our scale — depreciated capital, committed power, and a sunk decision that shapes next year's budget. Improving utilisation is highly reversible: if we build a better scheduler and it turns out we still need cards, nothing is wasted, because the scheduler makes the new cards cheaper to run too. When two options are close on expected value, the reversible one should usually win, and these options aren't even close.

Let's start with the case for buying. Our inference cluster runs hot during business hours and idle at night, and the queue depth during peak periods is real — people wait minutes for jobs that should take seconds. New hardware would immediately relieve that pressure, and there's something psychologically valuable about headroom: teams stop rationing their own experiments, and the friction that makes people avoid ML work in the first place disappears. Latency improves not just on average but at the tail, which is where user-facing pain actually lives. The p99 matters more than the mean, and more machines is the most direct way to move it.

But the directness is exactly what should make us pause. Capital spend on accelerators is the least reversible decision available to us. Depreciation on this class of hardware is brutal — the resale value of a GPU two generations later is a fraction of purchase price, and the generation cycle keeps compressing. If we buy now and our workload profile shifts, we're stuck holding silicon that's worth less every month we keep it. That's not an argument against ever buying; it's an argument that buying should be the option we exhaust last, not first.

Which brings us to utilisation. The honest diagnosis is that our current fleet is badly scheduled, not undersized. Nightly utilisation sits in the low single digits. Batch jobs that could run off-peak are run on-peak because it's convenient. Model weights are loaded cold on every request because nobody has finished the caching work. None of these are hard problems; they're unglamorous ones. A scheduler that deferrable jobs to the overnight window, aggressive weight caching, and a simple internal quota system would likely recover the equivalent of a meaningful fraction of a new node's capacity — at a cost measured in engineer-weeks rather than tens of thousands of dollars.

There's also an opportunity cost argument that cuts both ways, and I want to be fair to it. The counterargument to the utilisation path is that our engineers' time is the scarcest resource we have, and every week spent on scheduling infrastructure is a week not spent on the product. Hardware is bought with money we have; improvements are bought with attention we don't. I take that seriously. But I'd push back on the framing: the scheduling work is largely one-time, whereas the capacity problem is recurring. If we buy hardware now without fixing scheduling, we'll be back here in a year having paid twice — once in capital, once in the same queue-depth complaints, because the new machines will inherit the same 9-to-5 demand spike and the same idle nights.

Reliability cuts in favour of utilisation work too, though less obviously. A fleet that runs near capacity with no headroom is fragile — one node failure during peak turns into an outage rather than a slowdown. So the right utilisation project isn't just squeezing more throughput; it's building the queueing and prioritisation layer that lets us degrade gracefully. That's a capability we'd want even if we later buy hardware. In that sense the work is not an alternative to purchase but a prerequisite: whatever we decide in twelve months, the scheduler makes the fleet better.

So my recommendation: spend the next six to eight weeks on utilisation — off-peak scheduling, weight caching, and a lightweight quota system — and defer the purchase decision to the end of that window with real telemetry in hand. If peak p99 latency is still unacceptable after the fleet is genuinely well-used, we buy, and we'll buy with evidence rather than anxiety, and with a much sharper sense of exactly how much capacity we need.

Where am I uncertain? Genuinely, about how much of our peak pain is scheduling versus raw capacity. If the demand curve is spikier than I think, utilisation work will help the average but not the worst afternoons, and we'll have spent six weeks to learn we need hardware anyway. I think that's an acceptable risk — the scheduler work retains value regardless — but it's the assumption most likely to be wrong, and we should instrument for it from day one so the end-of-window decision is grounded in data, not opinion.

Happy to argue about this at Monday's sync.

Today, when a node goes down, we absorb its load because most machines are half-empty. If we run the fleet hot, a single hardware failure becomes a visible incident rather than a non-event. I take this seriously, but I think the answer is a deliberate target — say, 70 percent sustained utilisation with explicit reserve capacity — rather than the current situation, where our effective headroom is so large that we have stopped noticing we are paying for it. Reliability purchased with permanently idle hardware is reliability at a very high price.

**What I propose**

Concretely: we spend four to six weeks deploying a shared scheduler with preemption, instrument per-job and per-team utilisation properly, and set an internal cost signal so teams feel the true cost of reserved-but-idle capacity. We then re-measure. If, after that work, p95 wait times at our target utilisation still exceed our latency tolerance, we will have a defensible, quantified case for exactly how much hardware to buy — and we can buy it with confidence rather than instinct.

**Uncertainty**

I want to flag two things I could be wrong about. First, utilisation numbers can mislead; a fleet at 40 percent average may still be structurally short of a specific resource, such as high-memory cards for a particular workload, and no scheduler fixes that. Second, there is a real risk that the scheduling work takes longer or delivers less than I expect, in which case we will have spent a quarter and still need hardware. I accept that risk because the downside is a delayed purchase, whereas the reverse mistake — buying first — is much harder to undo.

I would like a decision by end of next week so we can start the scheduling work, or the procurement process, without losing more time. Happy to walk through the utilisation data in detail with anyone who wants to dig in.

# Memo: Buy More GPUs, or Use the Ones We Have Better?

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure working group
**Re:** Capacity decision for the local inference cluster

We've reached the point where our local AI hardware is running hot. Queue times during peak hours have crept up, batch jobs are competing with interactive workloads, and the natural instinct in the room is to buy more cards. I want to argue that we should spend the next quarter improving utilisation of what we already own before committing capital to new hardware, and that the argument rests less on the purchase price than on what we'd learn in the meantime.

The cost picture is the obvious starting point. New accelerators are expensive not just at purchase but across their whole life: power, cooling, rack space, and the engineering time to integrate and operate them. Our current fleet is far from saturated. Peak-hour utilisation looks high, but that's partly an artefact of how we schedule. Jobs are pinned to particular machines, batch work runs at whatever time someone happened to submit it, and several long-running experiments hold memory they're no longer using. If our true average utilisation across the week is in the range we estimate — somewhere between thirty and fifty percent — then a meaningful fraction of our peak demand could be absorbed by scheduling better, not by buying more. The cheapest capacity we can add is capacity we already own.

Latency is the counterargument, and it's a fair one. Interactive workloads suffer when they queue behind batch jobs, and no amount of clever scheduling fully eliminates that contention on a fixed pool. But this is precisely where utilisation work pays off: separating interactive and batch traffic, pre-empting low-priority jobs, and right-sizing model deployments would protect tail latency for the workloads people actually feel. Buying more hardware would also help, of course, but it helps by brute force, and it locks us into a capacity profile tuned to today's workload mix. If our inference patterns shift — and they have shifted twice in the past year — dedicated new machines optimised for the old pattern become stranded assets.

Reliability cuts both ways, and I want to be honest about that. A larger fleet gives us redundancy; if one node fails, work redistributes. A tightly utilised smaller fleet has less slack, so a single failure hurts more. That said, our current reliability problems are mostly self-inflicted: failed jobs that hold resources until someone notices, no automatic draining of unhealthy nodes, and no clear picture of which machines are actually degraded. Fixing those is prerequisite work either way. If we can't keep six nodes healthy through good hygiene, twelve nodes won't save us; they'll just fail more expensively.

The opportunity cost is where I think the case is strongest. Engineering time is our scarcest resource, and every week spent procuring, racking, and integrating new hardware is a week not spent on the product work that justifies our existence. Utilisation improvements — a proper scheduler, better queueing, telemetry that tells us where capacity actually goes — are work we need to do regardless. If we buy hardware first, we'll still have to do that work eventually, and we'll have paid for the privilege of doing it under pressure. If we do the work first, we either discover we don't need the purchase, or we make it later with a much sharper sense of exactly what to buy and how much.

There's also the question of reversibility. Hardware purchases are nearly irreversible at our scale; the resale market for used accelerators is thin, and depreciation is steep. Scheduling and telemetry work is almost entirely reversible — if it turns out we were wrong, we've lost some engineering weeks and gained a permanently better understanding of our own systems. When two options are close on expected value, the reversible one should win, because it preserves our ability to correct course.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. Our utilisation numbers are estimates, not measurements; it's possible that a proper telemetry pass reveals we really are saturated and the fleet is genuinely too small for the demand we face. That's a real possibility, and if the data shows it, we should buy — quickly and without guilt. But that's exactly the point: we should let the measurement decide, not the queue-time frustration of a bad week. The risk of waiting a quarter is some continued friction for heavy users. The risk of buying first is spending significant capital on capacity we may not need, while deferring the operational maturity that would make any fleet, of any size, actually perform.

**Recommendation:** Spend the next quarter on utilisation — telemetry, scheduling, and workload separation — with an explicit checkpoint at the end. If measured saturation justifies it, we proceed to procurement with a precise, evidence-based sizing. My expectation is that we'll end up buying less than we think we need today, and operating whatever we own considerably better.

Happy to discuss at Thursday's sync.

**MEMO**

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Working Group
**Re:** GPU capacity — buy more, or use what we have better?
**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

Over the past few months we've been bumping against the limits of our local inference hardware. Batch queues back up during peak hours, some experiments get deferred, and the natural instinct is to reach for a purchase order. Before we do that, I want to argue that we should spend the next quarter getting more out of the hardware we already own, and treat new purchases as a decision we make later, with better information.

The case for buying more capacity is real, and I don't want to strawman it. Our utilisation numbers show the fleet is genuinely saturated during business hours, and queue latency is the most visible symptom. When a researcher has to wait forty minutes for a fine-tuning job that would take twelve minutes on an idle card, that's not just an inconvenience — it's a tax on iteration speed, and iteration speed is the thing a team our size competes on. There's also a reliability argument: we run close enough to capacity that a single node failure degrades service noticeably. Redundancy is cheap insurance when you're already buying.

But the cost side of the ledger is less favourable than it first appears. The sticker price of accelerators is only the beginning. Add power, cooling, rack space, the engineering time to integrate and monitor new hardware, and the depreciation on chips that may be worth substantially less in three years, and the true cost per useful GPU-hour is considerably higher than our current amortisation line suggests. Meanwhile, our own telemetry tells a more interesting story: peak saturation coexists with long overnight and weekend troughs where utilisation drops below fifteen percent. We don't have a capacity problem so much as a scheduling and allocation problem. The hardware we need, in some sense, already exists — it's just in the wrong place at the wrong time.

That reframing matters because of opportunity cost. Every dollar we spend on metal we don't fully use is a dollar not spent on the things that actually differentiate us: better evaluation pipelines, cleaner data, more experiments shipped. Buying capacity is the easiest lever to pull and the least interesting one. The harder levers — smarter batching, quantised models where full precision isn't needed, priority queues that reflect real project value rather than whoever shouted loudest, a reservation system that lets us shift batch workloads into the troughs — cost engineering time, but that time is largely a one-off investment rather than a recurring liability. And unlike a purchase, these improvements compound: a scheduler we build this quarter keeps paying dividends after the hardware it optimises is long retired.

There's also the question of reversibility, which I think we've undervalued in past decisions. Buying hardware is close to irreversible. Resale markets for used accelerators are thin, our procurement cycle is slow, and once a purchase is in the budget it tends to stay in. Improving utilisation, by contrast, is highly reversible. If we tune the scheduler and it turns out we were wrong — if genuine demand growth means we're still saturated at eighty-five percent utilisation around the clock — we've lost a quarter of optimisation effort and gained a much sharper case for the purchase, with real numbers behind it. If we buy first and we're wrong, we've sunk capital into equipment that hums in a corner at twenty percent utilisation, and we'll feel obliged to invent workloads to justify it.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. Our demand forecast is genuinely fuzzy. If the new product initiative lands the way the roadmap hopes, inference load could double within two quarters, and no amount of scheduling cleverness will absorb that. There's also a lead-time risk: if we decide in six months that we do need hardware, we may face a procurement delay that a purchase made today would have avoided. Those are real risks, and I don't think we can price them precisely. But they argue for a trigger-based approach, not an immediate purchase: define the utilisation and queue-latency thresholds at which we commit to buying, monitor them weekly, and pull the trigger without re-litigating the whole debate if we cross them.

So my recommendation is this: spend the next quarter on utilisation — scheduling, batching, model optimisation, and honest measurement of demand — while pre-negotiating a purchase path we can execute quickly if the thresholds trip. That sequencing costs us little, preserves our options, and means that if we do buy, we'll be buying because the data says so rather than because the queues were annoying one Tuesday.

I'd welcome pushback, particularly from anyone closer to the product timeline than I am.

— Sent on behalf of the working group

# Memo: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?

**To:** Engineering team
**From:** Infra lead
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been running hot on our local inference hardware for about six weeks now. Queue times during peak hours have crept from seconds to minutes, and two of our internal tools have started timing out under load. The obvious question on the table is whether we buy more GPUs or find a way to get more out of the machines we already own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the answer is less obvious than it looks, and I'd like us to decide together before the next budget cycle closes.

Let's start with the case for buying. Our utilisation numbers tell a fairly clear story: we're sitting around 85–90% peak utilisation on the two workhorse boxes, which is genuinely high for inference workloads. At that level, small spikes in demand translate directly into queueing delays, because there's no headroom to absorb bursts. Buying a third machine would drop us to a more comfortable regime, roughly 60% peak, and would also give us something we currently lack entirely: redundancy. Right now, if one of our two GPUs fails or needs maintenance, we lose half our capacity instantly. That's a real reliability risk, and it's the strongest argument on the buy side. The cost is roughly $30–40k up front plus power, cooling, and rack space, which is material for a team our size but not existential.

The case for improving utilisation is subtler but worth taking seriously. Our off-peak utilisation is under 20%, which means the hardware we own is idle most of the day. Some of that is structural — demand simply clusters around working hours — but not all of it. We haven't done serious work on batching efficiency, model quantisation, or request scheduling, and my rough estimate is that better batching alone could cut peak load by 15–25%. There's also the question of whether some of our batch workloads could shift to off-peak windows entirely. If we can get peak utilisation down to 70% through software work, we buy ourselves breathing room at near-zero capital cost.

Here's where opportunity cost enters. The engineering time to do the utilisation work properly is real — I'd estimate four to six weeks of one senior engineer's focus, possibly more if we touch the scheduler. That's time not spent on the product roadmap, and given our current priorities, that's a genuine trade-off, not free money. Conversely, the capital spent on a new GPU is capital not spent on hiring, which is the other thing we keep saying we need. Neither resource is abundant enough that we can pretend the choice is costless.

The reversibility question tips the balance, I think. Buying hardware is largely irreversible at our scale. GPUs depreciate, resale is messy, and once the purchase is made, we've locked in our capacity trajectory for a year or more. Software improvements, by contrast, are fully reversible and compound: better batching and scheduling pay off on whatever hardware we own, including hardware we might buy later. If we do the software work first and it turns out to be insufficient, we've lost some time but gained knowledge and permanent efficiency gains. If we buy first and it turns out we didn't need to, we've spent $35k on a machine that idles at 15% utilisation like its siblings.

So my recommendation is: do the utilisation work first, on a strict six-week timebox, and treat the hardware purchase as the planned fallback rather than the default. Concretely, that means one engineer owns batching and scheduling improvements, we re-measure peak utilisation at the end of the window, and if we're still above 80% peak with degraded latency, we submit the purchase request with the data in hand. I'd also suggest we pre-approve the purchase in principle now, so the fallback isn't delayed by another budget cycle if the software work falls short.

I want to be honest about the uncertainty here. My estimate of achievable gains from batching is just that — an estimate — and if the real number is 5% rather than 20%, the timebox will have cost us six weeks of runway on a problem that's actively degrading. There's also a scenario where demand grows fast enough that even a third machine is a stopgap, in which case we should know that sooner rather than later. The timebox is designed to surface both of those outcomes quickly.

Happy to argue about this in Thursday's sync. If anyone has data on our actual latency SLOs or a better model of demand growth, bring it — this decision deserves better numbers than my back-of-envelope ones.

We've reached the point in our capacity planning where the obvious question has stopped being obvious. Our GPU fleet is running hot during business hours, queue times for inference jobs have crept into the tens of seconds, and the instinct in the room is to buy our way out. I want to argue, carefully, that we should not do that yet — or at least not primarily. The stronger move is to spend the next quarter squeezing real utilisation out of the hardware we already own, and to hold the purchase decision open until we have evidence that demand, not waste, is what's driving the shortage.

Start with the economics, because they're less favourable than they first appear. A new node isn't just its sticker price. There's power and cooling, rack space we'd need to negotiate for, the operational burden of integrating it into our scheduling stack, and — less tangibly — the depreciation risk that comes with hardware that ages fast in a market moving this quickly. Against that, our own telemetry tells a humbler story: our fleet averages somewhere in the low-forties percent utilisation over a full day, with sharp peaks mid-morning and after deployment windows. That gap between average and peak is where the real capacity lives. If we can lift the floor even modestly — better batching, smarter queue prioritisation, offloading batch jobs to overnight windows — we buy headroom that costs engineering time rather than capital. Engineering time is not free, but it's the one resource we can reallocate next sprint, and unlike a server, it doesn't sit on a balance sheet depreciating while we figure out whether we needed it.

Latency is the honest counterargument, and I don't want to wave it away. Some of our queue pain is structural: interactive inference requests genuinely do contend with long-running fine-tuning jobs, and no amount of overnight scheduling fixes a user waiting at 10:30 a.m. But even here, utilisation work helps. Preemption, request coalescing, and reserving a small slice of capacity for latency-sensitive paths are all changes that improve tail latency *without* new hardware. If after those changes our p99s are still unacceptable, that's a finding, not a failure — it becomes the evidence that justifies the purchase with numbers instead of frustration.

Reliability cuts both ways, and it's worth being candid about that. More nodes means more redundancy: today, a single hardware failure takes a meaningful fraction of our capacity with it, and that's a real operational risk. Buying hardware is, among other things, buying insurance. But insurance bought at the wrong price is just expense, and redundancy can also be improved by reducing how hard we run the machines we have — lower sustained utilisation means lower thermal stress, fewer failures, and more slack to absorb a dead node. The reliability argument for purchasing is strongest only after we've established that our baseline demand genuinely exceeds what a well-run fleet can carry.

The opportunity-cost question is the one I keep returning to. Every dollar we put into hardware this quarter is a dollar not spent on the product work that actually justifies this infrastructure existing. And there's a subtler cost: attention. A purchase decision made now, under queue-time pressure, tends to anchor the team's thinking around capacity as the solution to every performance problem. A quarter spent on utilisation builds a muscle — instrumentation, scheduling discipline, honest measurement — that pays off regardless of what we eventually buy. If we do buy, we'll buy less, and with better justification.

Which brings me to reversibility, the quiet tiebreaker. Buying hardware is nearly irreversible at our scale: resale value is poor, commitments to power and space are sticky, and the decision is hard to unwind if demand shifts. Improving utilisation is the opposite — every intervention is a small, reversible experiment, and the knowledge compounds even if individual changes are rolled back. When one path is cheap to undo and the other isn't, and when our evidence for the necessity of the irreversible path is still soft, the choice of sequencing writes itself.

So the recommendation: commit the next quarter to a utilisation programme with explicit targets — raise average utilisation, cut p99 queue times, and instrument everything so the results speak for themselves. Set a review date at the end of that quarter. If demand has grown faster than our improvements, we buy, and we'll do it with a precise picture of exactly how much we need and why. If the numbers show we were leaving capacity on the table, we'll have saved real money and learned something durable.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty honestly. I could be wrong about how much headroom is recoverable; some of our low utilisation may be irreducible fragmentation, and if so, the quarter's work will reveal that too, and the purchase case will be stronger

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering leadership
**From:** Infrastructure working group
**Re:** Recommendation on our inference capacity decision

**Summary**

We currently operate a small fleet of accelerators that, by our own telemetry, sits idle or underloaded for most of any given day. The question in front of us is whether to purchase additional local hardware to absorb projected demand, or to invest engineering time in raising the utilisation of what we already own. My recommendation is that we spend the next quarter improving utilisation first, and defer any purchase decision until we have real evidence that demand exceeds what a well-run fleet can supply.

**The case for utilisation first**

The strongest argument is economic. New hardware is a capital commitment that lands on our books immediately, while the demand it is meant to serve is still a forecast. Our own measurements suggest peak utilisation rarely exceeds forty percent, and the peaks are driven largely by batch workloads that we schedule for convenience rather than necessity. If we can shift and consolidate that work, we may discover that our existing fleet can handle two or three times the current load. Every point of utilisation we gain is capacity we acquire at near-zero capital cost, funded only by engineering hours we would in part be spending anyway on operational hygiene.

There is also a latency argument that cuts in favour of better scheduling rather than more metal. Adding hardware does not automatically make interactive requests faster; if our latency problems stem from queueing behind batch jobs, contention for memory, or inefficient batching, a larger fleet simply reproduces those problems at greater expense. Fixing the scheduler, right-sizing our batching, and separating latency-sensitive traffic from throughput work will do more for tail latency than a purchase order will.

Reliability, too, argues for consolidation before expansion. A larger fleet means more failure domains, more driver and firmware drift, more nodes to patch, and a longer mean time to repair when something breaks at 2 a.m. If we cannot currently keep a handful of machines healthy and observable, doubling the fleet doubles the surface area of that problem. Conversely, if we invest in better health checks, graceful draining, and automated recovery now, we make any future fleet — ours or a rented one — more dependable.

**The case for buying, and why it can wait**

I want to be fair to the other side. There is a real opportunity cost to under-provisioning: if a promising project stalls because it cannot get GPU time, the lost momentum may cost more than the hardware would have. Hardware lead times are long, and waiting too long means we could be caught flat when demand arrives. There is also a genuine risk that utilisation work turns out to be a distraction — a quarter of scheduler tuning that yields a ten percent gain while demand doubles underneath us.

These concerns are legitimate, but they are arguments for sequencing, not for buying now. The purchase is largely irreversible in the way that matters to us: capital spent on accelerators is capital not spent elsewhere, the hardware depreciates quickly in a fast-moving market, and reselling it recovers only a fraction of cost. Utilisation work, by contrast, is highly reversible. If we spend six weeks on scheduling and batching and discover the fleet genuinely cannot stretch, we have lost little — the observability, the cleaner workload separation, and the better failure handling all remain valuable regardless of what we buy afterwards. The information alone is worth the effort: a purchase decision made with measured demand curves and a tuned fleet is a far better decision than one made from a forecast and a feeling.

**What I propose**

Concretely, we should spend the next six to eight weeks on three fronts: instrumenting per-workload utilisation so our numbers stop being estimates; separating interactive and batch traffic so latency-sensitive requests stop queueing behind bulk jobs; and consolidating scheduled work into windows that keep the fleet busy without contending with itself. We should set a trigger in advance — for example, sustained utilisation above a defined threshold with queue times that violate our latency targets — so that the follow-on purchase decision is mechanical rather than political.

**Uncertainty**

I want to be honest about what we do not know. Our utilisation figures come from coarse telemetry and may understate contention at peak. Demand forecasts are soft, and a single new customer or internal project could change the picture quickly. If that happens, we should not let sunk effort in optimisation become a reason to delay a purchase the data clearly supports. The goal is not to avoid buying hardware forever; it is to buy it once, deliberately, with evidence in hand.

My recommendation stands: optimise first, buy second, and let the measurements make the second decision for us.

Our fleet sits at roughly 30–35% utilisation by most measures we can currently observe, though I want to be careful with that figure, because our measurement is part of the problem. We have no per-job accounting, no queueing telemetry worth the name, and our only real visibility is a dashboard someone checks occasionally and a shared belief that "the cluster feels idle most afternoons." That belief may well be true. But we are contemplating a capital purchase on the strength of a feeling, and that should make us uneasy.

The case for buying more hardware is straightforward and I don't want to dismiss it. Local capacity means predictable latency for our interactive workloads, no surprise egress or API price changes, and data that never leaves our perimeter. If a competitor or an internal deadline forces us to scale inference traffic quickly, waiting on procurement lead times could be genuinely painful. Hardware we own is also, in a narrow sense, an asset: it depreciates but it doesn't churn, and it insulates us from vendor pricing decisions we don't control.

But the case for better utilisation is stronger right now, for reasons that cut across cost, risk, and flexibility.

**Cost and opportunity cost**

A new node is not just its invoice price. It carries rack space, power, cooling, maintenance attention, and — most expensively — the engineering hours to integrate, monitor, and operate it. Our team is small. Every week someone spends racking hardware is a week they aren't spending on the product work that actually differentiates us. Meanwhile, the utilisation work — a proper scheduler, batch queueing for non-urgent jobs, time-slicing between interactive and offline workloads, honest per-team accounting — is work we would need to do eventually even if we buy more machines. Buying hardware without fixing utilisation means paying twice: once for capacity we won't use well, and again later for the tooling we skipped.

There's also a subtler opportunity cost. Idle capacity we already own is capital we've already spent; raising its yield is nearly free at the margin. Idle capacity we're about to buy is capital we're choosing to spend before we've demonstrated we can use the capacity we have. If we can't push our current fleet past 50% with a quarter of focused effort, that itself is a finding — it suggests our workloads are bursty in ways that more hardware won't smooth, and that we should be looking at hybrid or burst-to-cloud arrangements instead.

**Latency and reliability**

The strongest technical argument for more hardware is tail latency: when the fleet is saturated, interactive requests queue behind batch jobs and users feel it. But saturation is a scheduling failure as much as a capacity failure. Right now a single long-running job can monopolise a card that an interactive request needs. Preemption, sensible priority classes, and partitioning interactive from batch workloads would address most of our latency complaints at a fraction of the cost of new silicon. Reliability, similarly, improves more from redundancy in scheduling and better failure handling than from raw node count — though I'll concede that a larger fleet does make single-node failures less catastrophic, and that's a real point in favour of expansion eventually.

**Reversibility**

This is the decisive consideration for me. Utilisation work is highly reversible: if we build a scheduler and it turns out we were wrong about our headroom, we've lost a quarter of one engineer's time and gained permanent operational tooling. Buying hardware is largely irreversible at our scale: resale value on specialised accelerators is poor, the operating costs are committed, and the floor space is gone. When two options are plausibly similar in benefit, the reversible one should win, because it preserves our ability to be wrong cheaply.

**What I'm uncertain about**

I want to be honest about the limits of this recommendation. If our utilisation numbers are badly wrong — if the fleet is actually at 70% during the windows that matter and idle only when nobody needs it — then the utilisation project will hit a wall quickly, and we should pivot to procurement without embarrassment. I also can't rule out a near-term external event, a customer commitment or a demo

**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better**

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Inference capacity planning for the next two quarters

We've been running into capacity ceilings on our local inference hardware during peak hours, and the question on the table is whether we should purchase additional machines or invest in squeezing more out of the fleet we already own. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this, because the right answer is less obvious than the queue times make it look.

The case for buying is straightforward and emotionally compelling. Our p99 latency has degraded noticeably over the past month, and the team feels it every day. Waiting on a GPU is a tax on every experiment, every evaluation run, and every demo we give. New hardware would make that pain vanish immediately, and nobody has to do the unglamorous work of profiling, scheduling, and refactoring. There's also a genuine reliability argument: right now we have essentially no headroom, so a single hardware failure or a stuck job can take down workloads that have nothing to do with it. Redundancy is a real benefit, not a luxury.

But when I look at our actual utilization numbers, the case weakens considerably. Our fleet sits at roughly 35–40% average utilization across the day, with sharp peaks around standup, mid-afternoon, and just after deploy windows. That pattern tells me our problem is not capacity in aggregate — it's allocation in time. We are paying for a peak we use a few hours a day and idling through the rest. Buying more hardware at current utilization would mean paying roughly double for a fleet that still spends most of its life half-asleep. That's the opportunity cost that worries me most: the capital we'd spend on machines we don't fully use is capital we can't spend on the evaluation tooling, the observability work, and the model experiments that would actually differentiate our product. Hardware is the least differentiated thing we could buy.

The alternative — improving utilization — is cheaper but not free. Most of the wins available to us are organizational rather than technical: batching small jobs, moving long-running batch work to overnight windows, setting per-team quotas so a single runaway evaluation can't monopolize the pool, and putting a real queue with priorities in front of the hardware instead of the current first-come free-for-all. None of this is novel engineering, but it does require sustained attention from people who are already stretched, and it will make some workflows slower in exchange for making the system as a whole faster. That trade is worth naming honestly: individual convenience will dip before collective latency improves. If we're not willing to enforce the queue, this path fails quietly and we end up buying hardware anyway, having lost a quarter.

There's also a reversibility asymmetry that I think should drive the decision. Buying hardware is close to irreversible at our scale. Machines depreciate, they consume rack space and power whether we use them or not, and reselling used accelerators is a hassle that recovers only a fraction of cost. Utilization work, by contrast, is almost perfectly reversible: if the queue and batching changes don't deliver, we've lost a few engineer-weeks and we can proceed to purchase with better data and, importantly, a better baseline to specify against. The option value of waiting is high precisely because the utilization work is cheap to attempt and informative even in failure. If we do the work and still see p99s above our target at sustained utilization above 70%, that is strong evidence the constraint is real and the purchase is justified — and we'll buy the right amount rather than guessing.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty here honestly. My utilization figures come from partial instrumentation, and it's possible that a meaningful fraction of our "idle" time is actually memory fragmentation or thermal throttling that no scheduler will fix. It's also possible that our workload mix is about to change — if the new retrieval pipeline lands as planned, our inference load could grow enough to make today's fleet genuinely insufficient regardless of scheduling. I don't think either risk changes the recommendation, but both should be checked within the first month of this work rather than assumed away.

**Recommendation:** Do not purchase additional hardware this quarter. Spend the next six weeks on the utilization program — queueing with priorities, overnight batch windows, per-team quotas, and better instrumentation — with a defined success threshold. If sustained utilization exceeds 70% and p99 latency still misses our target, we proceed to purchase with a concrete, evidence-based sizing, and I'll write that proposal myself. This sequencing costs us little, preserves the option to buy, and avoids paying twice for capacity we already own.

Happy to walk through the numbers in detail at Thursday's sync.

**To:** Platform Engineering Team
